samples.question: This picture shows exactly two grey pipes on a white page. Each pipe is one unbroken stroke built from three straight sections joined end to end, so each pipe has exactly two bends and exactly two loose ends. The two pipes never touch and never cross each other, so every stretch of grey belongs to one pipe only and you can follow either pipe from one of its loose ends to the other. A green disc covers one loose end of one of the two pipes; call that pipe the green-ended pipe. The other pipe has no green disc. There are four coloured squares, one red, one blue, one orange and one purple. Each square sits just outside exactly one bend, in the open corner on the outer side of that bend, separated from the grey stroke by a small gap, and each square is far nearer to its own pipe than to the other pipe, so a square belongs to whichever pipe runs beside it. Two of the four squares therefore mark the two bends of the green-ended pipe and the other two mark the two bends of the other pipe. A bend is sharper when the pipe changes direction there by a larger angle, that is, when the corner between its two sections is tighter; a bend is gentler when the pipe carries on more nearly straight. Only the two bends of the green-ended pipe are being compared. How the bends of the other pipe look, how long the sections are, which colours are used, where the pipes sit on the page and which square happens to lie nearest the green disc do not matter. Of the two squares that mark the bends of the green-ended pipe, which one marks the sharper bend? Answer red, blue, orange or purple.
